Neither depends on the type of document.
An unknown date is noted (n.d.).
k: Ibid. = same source as the note just before; op. cit. = a work already cited a few pages back.
h: Ibid is the twin next door; op. cit. is the cousin a few pages away.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – References: Ibid. and op. cit.

q: According to the course, how are appendices presented?
o: Numbered in Roman numerals, each with a title and separate pagination, and referred to in the text
Numbered in Arabic numerals and placed before the bibliography without titles
Merged into the theoretical chapters to save space
Placed before the introduction, after the abstract
e: Appendices are numbered in Roman numerals and referred to in the text with the necessary details ('see Annex I, page...'). They have separate pagination and each has a title. They include an example of the material used (questionnaire, scale, interview guide), an example of a participant's answer sheet, important statistical tables not included in the text, and the permission sheet for applying the material in the institution. Page numbers of the main text are Arabic.
w: Arabic numerals are for the main text's pages; appendices use Roman numerals and titles.
Appendices are separate from the theoretical chapters.
Appendices come at the very end, after the bibliography.
k: Appendices: Roman numerals, titled, separately paginated; contain instruments, an answer sheet, extra tables and permissions.
h: Annex I, II, III: Roman at the back.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – 9. Annexes

q: According to the course, the introduction of a dissertation has a funnel shape. What does this mean?
o: It moves from the general phenomenon to the specific context, objectives, problem and hypotheses
It starts with the results and ends with the general theory
It is written last and contains only the conclusion of the study
It lists all the bibliography references in narrowing order
e: The introduction goes from the general to the particular: introduce the phenomenon, place the research in its specific context, cite the most relevant theoretical facts and previous studies, and outline the organization of the dissertation. It then explains the objectives and motivation, the value of the research (theoretical interest: new information; practical interest: solutions to problems), presents the problem and formulates the hypotheses with operationally defined variables.
w: Results come much later, in Part 2.
The introduction opens the work; the conclusion is a separate section.
The bibliography is a separate section at the end.
k: Introduction = funnel: general phenomenon → context → previous studies → objectives, interest → problem → hypotheses.
h: Wide mouth, narrow spout.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Reminder of the parts of the research

q: How does the course define the theoretical and practical interest of a research project?
o: Theoretical interest: providing new information; practical interest: presenting solutions to problems
Theoretical interest: the researcher's hobbies; practical interest: the researcher's career
Theoretical interest: the number of references; practical interest: the number of participants
Theoretical interest: the statistics used; practical interest: the software used
e: In the introduction, after the objectives and motivations, the researcher explains the value of the research. The course defines theoretical interest as bringing new information (adding to knowledge) and practical interest as presenting solutions to problems (applications for clinicians, schools, families). Dr. Riachy's final exams ask for both explicitly in the introduction: 'explain its theoretical and practical importance'.
w: Personal interests belong to motivations, not to the research's interest.
Counts of references or participants are not what interest means.
Statistics and software belong to the analysis plan.
k: Theoretical interest = new knowledge; practical interest = solutions to real problems.
h: Theory adds knowledge; practice solves problems.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Introduction; RM final exams 2024–2026

q: In the course's 'Research steps', what does Part 2 (Methodological approach), Chapter 1 'Working method' contain?
o: Sample, methods and techniques, limitations, data collection, statistical processing
Conceptual framework, theories, definitions of the variables and empirical studies
Objectives, motivations, theoretical and practical interest, problem statement and hypotheses
Presentation of the results in tables, statistical tests and discussion of the results
e: The course's plan: Introduction (objectives and motivations, interest, problem, hypotheses with operational definitions); Part 1, Frame of reference (Chapter 1 conceptual and theoretical framework; Chapter 2 empirical framework); Part 2, Methodological approach (Chapter 1 working method: 1.1 sample, 1.2 methods and techniques, 1.3 limitations, 1.4 data collection, 1.5 statistical processing; Chapter 2 analysis and discussion of results); conclusion; bibliography; appendices.
w: These make up Part 1, the frame of reference.
These all belong to the introduction.
These form Chapter 2 of Part 2, analysis and discussion.
k: Part 2 Ch. 1 = sample, methods and techniques, limitations, data collection, statistical processing; Ch. 2 = analysis and discussion.
h: Who, how, limits, gathering, numbers.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Research steps

q: In Dr. Riachy's final exams, Question 1 asks you to develop a topic. What must Part 1, the frame of reference, contain?
o: A conceptual and theoretical framework, and an empirical framework
The sample, the methods and the techniques used
The objectives, motivations and theoretical and practical interest
The statistical results and their discussion
e: The 2024–2025 and 2025–2026 final exams all use the same structure. Introduction: objectives and motivations, theoretical and practical interest, problem, hypotheses with variables identified and operationally defined. Part 1, frame of reference: conceptual and theoretical framework, plus empirical framework (existing studies). Part 2, methodological approach: working method, with the sample, methods and techniques used. It mirrors the course's research steps.
w: Sample, methods and techniques belong to Part 2.
Objectives and interest belong to the introduction.
Results are not requested in the exam's development question.
k: Exam Q1: Introduction (aims, interest, problem, operational hypotheses) → Part 1 (theory + empirical studies) → Part 2 (sample, methods, techniques).
h: Intro, theory, method.
r: RM final exams 2024–2026 (Dr. Riachy) + Research Methodology course – Research steps

q: Exam title: 'The relationship between smartphone addiction and loneliness in adolescents.' Which type of research fits best according to the course?
o: Descriptive correlational quantitative research
Experimental research with a control group
Content analysis of documents
Cross-sectional comparison of different age groups
e: The title asks about a relationship between two measured variables, neither manipulated by the researcher. The course's correlational method 'measures the degree of relationship between two or more quantifiable variables', a descriptive quantitative technique. A fitting hypothesis would be operational, such as: 'There is a positive correlation between smartphone addiction scores and loneliness scores in adolescents.' Experimental research would require manipulating addiction, which is neither feasible nor ethical.
w: Nobody can ethically assign adolescents to become addicted, so no manipulation is possible.
The study measures adolescents, not documents.
The title concerns one age group, not a comparison of ages.
k: A title stating a 'relationship' between two measured variables calls for a descriptive correlational design.
h: 'Relationship' → correlate.
r: RM final exam 2024–2025, session 1 (Dr. Riachy) + Research Methodology course – Correlational method

q: Exam title: 'The influence of childhood trauma on adult attachment styles.' Why is an experimental design NOT appropriate?
o: Childhood trauma, the independent variable, cannot be manipulated, so groups are compared descriptively
Attachment style is the independent variable, and it cannot be measured with any instrument
Experiments are forbidden with adult participants under the course's ethical rules
The title contains no dependent variable, so no hypothesis can be formulated from it
e: The experimental method requires manipulating the IV and comparing treated and untreated groups. Childhood trauma is the IV and attachment style the DV, but trauma can only be measured, never induced. The researcher compares adults with and without a trauma history, a descriptive-comparative design, possibly with case studies. The course treats a similar title, 'The father's violence and its influence on the child's aggressive behaviour', the same way.
w: Attachment style is the DV, and it can be measured with scales or interviews.
Experiments with adults are possible; the problem is that trauma cannot be manipulated.
Experiments with adults are possible; the problem is that trauma cannot be induced.
k: When the IV is a past experience that cannot be manipulated (trauma, violence), use a descriptive-comparative design or case study.
h: You cannot assign trauma; you can only compare.
r: RM final exam 2024–2025, session 2 (Dr. Riachy) + Research Methodology course – Training

q: Exam title: 'The effects of meditation on stress reduction in workers.' Which is a correct directional operational hypothesis?
o: Workers who follow a meditation programme show lower stress scores than workers who do not
Meditation has an effect on stress
Is there a relationship between meditation and stress in workers?
There is no significant difference in stress between workers who meditate and those who do not
e: Here meditation is the IV and stress the DV, and an experimental design fits because a meditation programme can be applied to one group and not another. A directional operational hypothesis names concrete groups and predicts the direction with a term such as 'lower than'. 'Meditation has an effect on stress' is the general hypothesis; the question form is a research question; the 'no significant difference' form is the null hypothesis.
w: This is the general hypothesis: abstract, with no groups or direction.
This is a research question, not an affirmative hypothesis.
This is the null (statistical) hypothesis.
k: Directional operational hypothesis = concrete groups + measurable DV + direction word ('lower than').
h: Groups, measure, arrow.
r: RM final exam 2024–2025, session 1 (Dr. Riachy) + Research Methodology course – Hypotheses

q: Exam title: 'The role of intrinsic motivation in academic persistence among university students.' Identify the variables.
o: IV: intrinsic motivation; DV: academic persistence; population: university students
IV: academic persistence; DV: intrinsic motivation; population: university students
IV: university students; DV: intrinsic motivation; population: academic persistence
IV and DV: intrinsic motivation; population: academic persistence
e: The title states that intrinsic motivation plays a role in (acts on) academic persistence, so intrinsic motivation is the IV (the presumed cause or influence) and academic persistence is the DV (the outcome). University students are the population, not a variable. A general hypothesis would be 'Intrinsic motivation influences academic persistence'; an operational one: 'Students with high intrinsic motivation persist more than students with low intrinsic motivation.'
w: This reverses the cause (IV) and the effect (DV).
The population is never the IV, and persistence is a variable, not the population.
One variable cannot be both IV and DV in the same relationship.
k: In 'the role of X in Y among Z', X is the IV, Y the DV and Z the population.
h: The 'role' plays on the outcome.
r: RM final exam 2025–2026 (Dr. Riachy) + Research Methodology course – Variables

q: Exam title: 'The impact of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance.' Which type of research fits best?
o: Experimental: deprive one group of sleep and compare its cognitive performance with a control group
Content analysis of sleep diaries written by participants over several weeks of observation
Qualitative case study of 6 to 10 insomniac patients, without any comparison group
Cross-sectional comparison of the cognitive performance of several different age groups
e: The title asks about the impact (cause and effect) of sleep deprivation (IV) on cognitive performance (DV). Sleep deprivation can be manipulated under controlled conditions: one group is kept awake, the control group sleeps normally, other variables are held constant, and performance on cognitive tests is compared. The course's experimental method is designed exactly for establishing such cause-and-effect relationships between equivalent groups.
w: Content analysis processes documents and cannot test cause and effect.
A case study without a comparison group cannot test a causal impact.
The title involves no comparison of ages.
k: When the IV can be manipulated under controlled conditions and the title asks about impact, choose an experimental design.
h: Can you switch the IV on and off? Then experiment.
r: RM final exam 2024–2025, session 2 (Dr. Riachy) + Research Methodology course – Experimental method

q: In the course's training topic 'Emotional intelligence and academic performance of secondary students in Beirut', which method and instruments are proposed?
o: A comparative descriptive method with an EI test, academic results and a teacher questionnaire
An experimental method in which EI is trained in one class and compared with another class
A content analysis of the school textbooks used in the secondary classes of Beirut schools
A single case study of one student using a projective test and a clinical interview
e: In this worked example, emotional intelligence is the IV ('it is the cause, the stimulus, it acts and influences') and academic performance the DV. The research questions compare levels (high versus low EI) and groups (boys and girls, S1 and S3, public and private schools). The course proposes a comparative descriptive method to establish relationships between the two variables, with an EI test, students' academic results and a questionnaire for teachers.
w: No training programme is applied, so the design is not experimental.
The study measures students, not textbooks.
Many students and groups are compared; it is not a single case.
k: EI and academic performance: IV = EI, DV = performance; comparative descriptive method with an EI test, grades and a teacher questionnaire.
h: Measure, compare, relate.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Training: emotional intelligence

q: Classify: 'There is no significant difference in learning strategies between boys and girls.'
o: Null (statistical) hypothesis
Directional operational hypothesis
Non-directional operational hypothesis
General hypothesis
e: The course's training answer: this is a null hypothesis because it states that there is no relationship (no difference) between boys' and girls' learning strategies. The null hypothesis is the statistical form tested by inferential tests such as Student's t. A non-directional operational version would say 'There are significant differences in learning strategies between boys and girls'; a directional one would say which sex uses more strategies.
w: No direction is predicted; it denies any difference.
A non-directional hypothesis asserts that a difference exists.
A general hypothesis states an abstract relationship, not 'no difference'.
k: 'There is no significant difference/relationship' = null (statistical) hypothesis.
h: 'No' → null.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Training: types of hypotheses

q: Classify: 'As poverty increases, violence increases.'
o: Directional hypothesis, expressed as 'the more... the more'
Null hypothesis, because it does not mention any statistical test
Non-directional hypothesis, because no group is named
Zero-correlation hypothesis, because the two variables vary together
e: The course's training answer classifies this as a directional hypothesis because it is expressed as 'the more... the more': as one variable rises, so does the other, which predicts a positive relationship. Other direction markers in the course include 'more than', 'less than', 'better than', 'positive correlation' and 'negative correlation'. A non-directional form would merely say 'Poverty is related to violence'.
w: It asserts a relationship, so it is not null; null hypotheses deny any relationship or difference.
It predicts the direction (both increase together), so it is not non-directional.
Zero correlation means no relationship, the opposite of variables varying together.
k: 'The more X, the more Y' predicts a positive direction, so the hypothesis is directional.
h: Both arrows point up.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Training: types of hypotheses

q: Which formatting rule matches the course?
o: Body text in Times New Roman 12 pt, chapter titles centered in bold 16 pt capitals
Body text in Arial 14 pt, chapter titles in 12 pt italics aligned to the left margin
Footnotes in 12 pt, gathered at the end of each chapter rather than on the same page
Appendices numbered in Arabic numerals and main-text pages numbered in Roman numerals
e: The course's formatting rules: A4 paper, text justified left and right, Times New Roman 12 pt; page numbers in Arabic numerals (centered or right, top or bottom); appendices in Roman numerals; footnotes separated by a line, in 10 pt, entirely on the same page; part titles (theoretical, practical, appendices) on a separate page in bold capitals at 18 pt; chapter titles centered, bold capitals, 16 pt; a new page for each chapter; numbering 1., 1.1, 1.2.
w: The font is Times New Roman 12 and chapter titles are bold 16 pt.
Footnotes are 10 pt and on the same page.
This reverses the two numbering systems: pages are Arabic, appendices Roman.
k: Times New Roman 12; footnotes 10; chapter titles 16 bold; part titles 18 bold; Arabic page numbers; Roman appendices.
h: 12 text, 16 chapters, 18 parts, 10 footnotes.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – III. Formatting

q: What does the course say the abstract should contain?
o: In English and French, 1–15 lines: problem, sample, method, main results, interpretation, conclusion
Only the title of the dissertation, the researcher's name and the supervisor's name
A full copy of the questionnaire used and the raw data collected from every participant
The acknowledgments to the supervisor and the dedications to family and friends
e: The course lists the preliminary sections in order: cover page, title page, dedications, acknowledgments, contents (where pagination starts), list of figures, list of tables, and the abstract. The abstract is in English and French, 1 to 15 lines long, and includes the problem, the sample, the methodology, the main results, their interpretation and the conclusion. Some institutions also require about five keywords that best represent the research.
w: The title page, not the abstract, carries the title and names.
Instruments and raw data go in the appendices.
Dedications and acknowledgments are separate preliminary sections.
k: Abstract: English and French, 1–15 lines, problem, sample, method, main results, interpretation, conclusion; ~5 keywords.
h: The whole study in a paragraph.
r: Research Methodology course (Dr. Riachy) – Sections of the dissertation
